claims.text: Severe plastic deformation induces grain refinement in steel.
Grain refinement produced by severe plastic deformation increases the density of grain boundaries.
The increased density of grain boundaries provides additional nucleation sites for a passive oxide film.
Additional nucleation sites cause more rapid formation of the passive oxide film.
A refined grain structure increases the stability of the passive oxide film.
The passive oxide layer mitigates active corrosion.
Severe-plastic-deformation-refined steel will have a lower corrosion rate than coarse-grained steel tested under the same conditions.
Refined-grain steel will exhibit a higher passivation current density than coarse-grained steel.
Refined-grain steel will exhibit a lower corrosion current density than coarse-grained steel.
The proposed mechanism should apply to steels of similar chemical composition in moderate corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Very high temperatures or ultra-high chloride concentrations may prevent the predicted corrosion-resistance trend from holding.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement may depend on severe-plastic-deformation parameters and environmental conditions.
Microstructural changes caused by severe plastic deformation other than grain refinement may contribute to corrosion behavior.

contradictions.description: The mechanism invokes a more stable and protective passive film, but the predicted outcome includes higher passivation current density as an improvement. This direction is inconsistent with the usual interpretation that a lower passive-state current indicates less dissolution through a more protective film, and it is not reconciled with the alternative prediction of lower corrosion current density.
